result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.local_efficiency()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Calculate the local efficiency of the graph. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L29587-L29654){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.local_efficiency() ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Local efficiency](/assets/graphs/local-efficiency.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="The shared seven-node graph shaded by each node's local efficiency, how well its neighbors stay connected without it: A 1.00, B and D 0.83, C 0.72, E 0.33, F and G 0. The method returns the mean over all nodes, 0.53, highlighted at the bottom of the table." width="100%"} Local efficiency is the average global efficiency of each node's neighborhood subgraph. It measures how efficiently the neighbors of a node can communicate when that node is removed. High local efficiency indicates good redundancy and fault tolerance. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The average local efficiency (between 0 and 1). ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} For every node $v$, the local efficiency measures how well its neighborhood $N(v)$ can route around it: $E_{\mathrm{loc}}(v) = E_{\mathrm{glob}}(G[N(v)])$, the global efficiency of the induced subgraph on $v$'s neighbors, and the overall statistic is the average across all nodes. Nodes with $|N(v)| < 2$ contribute $0$ by convention since there is nothing to route. High local efficiency signals a network with redundant local paths, which is closely related to clustering but sensitive to path lengths rather than just adjacency: a cycle among the neighbors gives higher local efficiency than an adjacent chain even though both are equally clustered. Total cost is $O(V \cdot \bar{k}(\bar{k} + \bar{e}))$ where $\bar{k}$ and $\bar{e}$ are average neighborhood sizes and edge counts. ## Examples {.doc-examples} In a complete graph, removing any node still leaves its neighbors fully connected to each other, so local efficiency is at its maximum of 1.0: ::: {#f00b55f0 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph() n = 5 for i in range(n): graph.add_node(label=f"n{i}") nodes = sorted(graph.get_node_ids()) for i in range(n): for j in range(i + 1, n): graph.add_edge(nodes[i], nodes[j]) # Returns 1.0 graph.local_efficiency() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 1.0 ``` ::: ::: A star graph has very low local efficiency: every leaf's only neighbor is the hub, so leaves have no way to reach each other once the hub is set aside, unlike a cycle where neighbors retain redundant paths: ::: {#13a0b003 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} star = ec.Graph() star.add_star_graph(10) cycle = ec.Graph() cycle.add_cycle_graph(10) # Star's local efficiency is much lower than the cycle's (star.local_efficiency(), cycle.local_efficiency()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (0.0, 0.0) ``` ::: :::
